newsitem.title: UK: Huge UK jobless fall points to January rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Huge UK jobless fall points to January rate rise.

text.p: A massive fall in British unemployment in November clearly shows the labour market is tightening, the economy is growing fast and interest rates are set to rise early next year, analysts said on Wednesday.

"The data are consistent with considerable labour market tightening and reinforce the view that the economy is growing very strongly and monetary policy is too loose," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch. "The chances of a rate rise on January 15 are now very high."
UK unemployment fell by 95,800 in November.
This was the largest monthly fall since records began in 1971 and pushed the unemployment level below the pschologically important two million level for the first time since early 1991.
Stewart said the data matches survey evidence which shows employers are finding it increasingly difficult to find staff.
"The CBI and BCC have both reported recruitment difficulties and it is safe to say earnings are not going to stay as subdued next year as they have been this year."
The growth of underlying average earnings stayed steady at 4.0 percent in October.
But other economists said slower wage growth in the manufacturing may help offset the more generous pay rises seen in the services sector for some months ahead.
In the year to October, average earnings in the services sector picked up by a quarter point to 4.0 percent but in the manufacturing sector they ticked down a quarter point to 4.25 percent.

"The latest settlement data show that, if anything, settlements have dropped. That should help to offset the big rises coming through in the financial services sector over the next few months," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS.
While the huge monthly fall in the jobless total suggests more jobs are being created, sweeping change to the benefits system mean economists are reluctant to take the fall at face value.

The government replaced unemployment benefit with the Job Seekers' Allowance in October and the backlog of claims at job centres exaggerated the fall by around 20,000, the Office for National Statistics said. Changes to means-testing knocked another 5,000 off the jobless total, the ONS said and associated changes to postal claims also exaggerated the overall fall, although the ONS would not estimate its effect.
Latest figures on job creation cover the three months to September and showed 165,000 new jobs were created in the period, including among the self-employed.
"Over the last couple of quarters we have seen seen employment picking up which is what you'd expect," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

"But if the recent trend has continued, it is likely an awful lot of them are in the part time sector. There is a danger that, combined with all the distortions from the JSA, the big falls in unemployment are exaggerating the growth picture."
